answer.generated: The four levels of ANSI transaction isolation—Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Repeatable Read, and Serializable—differ in their approach to ensuring the consistency and integrity of concurrent transactions, akin to how process synchronization mechanisms manage access to shared resources in operating systems. Read Uncommitted, the weakest form of isolation, allows reading uncommitted changes, much like a process might access a shared resource without any locks, potentially leading to dirty reads similar to a deadlock when multiple processes attempt to access the same resource simultaneously. Read Committed ensures that transactions only read committed data, analogous to mutual exclusion where only one process can access a resource at a time, preventing inconsistent states but allowing non-repeatable reads. Repeatable Read further isolates transactions so they cannot read uncommitted data, similar to a lock held during the entire duration of a transaction to prevent other processes from modifying the resource, thus avoiding phantom reads. Serializable is the strongest form of isolation, where transactions appear to execute serially, ensuring no interference between concurrent transactions, much like a full mutual exclusion protocol where all processes must wait until another finishes before starting, guaranteeing no deadlocks or inconsistencies. However, achieving serializability can be resource-intensive and may lead to increased contention, similar to the overhead of maintaining locks in an operating system to avoid deadlocks.
